newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Belgium to campaign for broader NATO expansion-PM.
newsitem.headline: Belgium to campaign for broader NATO expansion-PM.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said on Friday that NATO had been too political in selecting candidates for early expansion and pledged to seek the inclusion of five new members this year, including Romania.
Dehaene's support added to a list of NATO members backing Romania's bid to overcome long odds and win early entry alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic.
France, Italy, other Mediterranean states and Canada support Romania, but the United States and Britain have given no public backing. Slovenia is also seen as a longshot chance.

Dehaene acknowledged that no decision had been taken on which candidates would be asked to join at NATO's July summit in Madrid. But he said the apparent consensus to limit initial expansion to three states was based on "less objective" criteria than those for enlarging the European Union.
"We favour a wider first-wave enlargement rather than one limited to three countries as defended by some," Dehaene told a news conference after two days of talks with Romanian leaders.

"Romania's bid must be taken into account as it easily meets all the conditions, which unfortunately have been less objective for NATO than for the European Union. The (NATO) decision has taken on a more political and less objective dimension."

Romania's initialling last week of a post-communist treaty with the former Soviet republic of Ukraine, its north-eastern neighbour, was "an especially important factor" in boosting its chances, he said.
Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, whose government defeated ex-communists in last year's election, said Bucharest would "fight to the last moment for first-wave admission".
Dehaene said expansion had to be done openly and on the basis of an accord being drawn up with Russia to persuade Moscow to drop objections to its former Warsaw Pact allies joining the Alliance.
Russia appears to have accepted the principle of expansion and is concentrating on winning concessions on deployment of troops in eastern Europe and on having a say in NATO planning.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin said this week the accord was nearly complete and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana is to resume talks in Moscow next week with the aim of having the treaty signed in Paris on May 27.
Dehaene said unsuccessful first-wave candidates should be told clearly when and in what conditions they might be considered again.
"If it turns out that there is no consensus on (broader expansion), we believe that clear conditions must be defined for countries not included in the first wave," he said.

"This concerns not only the fact that there will be a second wave, but the conditions and time frame in which it will occur. There could well be an impression that those not in the first group have been rejected."
